textbookText: Unique features Most diversified, Presence of jointed appendages, metamerically segmented, haemocoelomate, shedding off outer cuticle frequently, body divided into head, thorax and abdomen or cephalothorax and abdomen, open circulatory system, compound eye, larval form in the most.

Classification Classification of phylum arthropoda is controversial and complicated which is divided into seven subphyla but the true arthropods belong to the three sub-phyla namely trilobitomorpha, chelicerata and mandibulata. Among them, trilobitomorpha is not mentioned here as it comprises extinct arthropods.

Sub-phylum: Chelicerata (Gr; chele-claw; keros-horn)
Body is divided into cephalothorax and abdomen, presence of six pair of appendages in total and absence of antenna are the main features. This subphylum consists of two classes:
Class 1: Merostomata (Meros-thigh, stoma mouth)

i. All found in marine water, simple eyes in median position and compound eyes are placed laterally. ii. They have 5-6 pairs of abdominal appendages; with book gills for respiration. iii. Excretion takes place by coxal glands. iv. Abdomen ends at sharp telson.
Example: Limulus (king crab or horse shoe crab; a living fossil)

Class 2: Arachnida i. They are mostly terrestrial, few are aquatic. ii. They have only simple eyes. iii. Cephalothorax is with a pair of chelicerae, a pair of pedipalpi and four pair of walking legs. No appendages from abdomen. iv. Excretion occurs by coxal glands and malpighian tubules. v. Respiration by tracheae and book lungs or book gills. vi. They have no antenna and wings. vii. They are carnivorous and hence predator.
Example: Aranea (spider), Palamnaeus (scorpion), ticks, mites etc.

Sub-phylum: Mandibulata (L; mandibula-mandible; ata-group)

They are both terrestrial and aquatic, body divided as head, thorax and abdomen or cephalothorax and abdomen, presence of compound eyes and 3-5 pairs of appendages in head. This subphylum consists of three classes:

Class: 3 Crustacea ( L; crusta-shell) i. They are mostly aquatic and few are terrestrial (wood louse), respire by gills. ii. Body is divisible as cephalothorax and abdomen where cephalothorax is covered by hard carapace and segmented abdomen by sclerites. iii. Head is five segmented and each segment bears biramous (two branched) appendages. iv. Sexes are separate with sexual dimorphism. v. Development is direct and indirect both.
Example: Palaemon (prawn), Cancer (crab), lobster, shrimp, copepod, water flea etc.

Class 4: Myriapoda (Gr; myrios- terrestrial; podos-foot) i. They are exclusively terrestrial and air breathing forms. ii. Body is divisible into head and trunk. Trunk is many segmented and each segment bear paired jointed legs. iii. They have a pair of antennae, three pair of jaws and more than 11 pair of legs. iv. Breathing occurs through trachea. Trachea opens outside through small pores called spiracles. v. They excrete through malpighian tubules. vi. Sexes are separate.
Example: Julus (millipede), Scolopendra (centipede), Spirobolus, Pauropus etc.

Class 3: Insecta (L; insectus- cut or divided) i. They are mostly terrestrial, aerial and air breathing forms. ii. Body is divisible into head thorax and abdomen. iii. Head bears paired compound eyes, antennae, mandibles and two pairs of maxillae. iv. Mouth parts are modified according to their feeding habit. v. There is three pair of walking legs arising laterally from thorax and wings are two pair or 1 pair or absent. vi. Respiration occurs by branched tracheae which open externally through spiracles. vii. Excretion by malpighian tubules. viii. Sexes are separate, fertilization is internal and development is direct and indirect both. Indirect development with larval forms and metamorphosis. Direct development with immature young one resembling adult is called nymph.
Example: Pieris (butterfly), Bombyx (silkworm), Melanopus (grasshopper), Periplaneta (cockroach), Apis (honey bee), Musca (house fly) etc.
